abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a unified information-theoretic framework for nonlinear signal processing that fundamentally reconceptualizes how statistical signal processing approaches handle higher-order statistical structures in complex signal environments. Traditional methods rely on second-order statistics and Gaussian assumptions, which fail to capture the full complexity of real-world signals exhibiting non-Gaussian behavior and nonlinear dynamics. The proposed framework establishes rigorous connections between information-theoretic measures—including entropy, mutual information, and generalized divergence metrics—and kernel-based representations of nonlinear signal transformations. We derive novel theoretical bounds demonstrating that the proposed approach achieves information-theoretic optimality for a broad class of nonlinear signal processing problems, including signal denoising, feature extraction, and signal separation. The theoretical analysis reveals fundamental limitations of existing approaches and provides new insights into the trade-offs between computational complexity and statistical efficiency. A critical contribution is the establishment of minimax optimality conditions that characterize the relationship between kernel bandwidth selection and estimation accuracy in finite-sample regimes. The framework enables the development of new algorithms with provable performance guarantees, representing a paradigm shift in how nonlinear signal processing theory addresses the challenge of extracting meaningful information from complex signal structures.

This paper presents a significant theoretical advancement in adaptive filter theory by developing a unified convergence analysis framework that substantially improves upon existing results for normalized least-mean-square algorithms operating under non-stationary conditions. While conventional analysis approaches rely on independence assumptions that are violated in practical implementations, the proposed framework provides rigorous convergence guarantees without requiring these restrictive assumptions. We introduce novel energy bounding techniques that enable precise characterization of the transient and steady-state behavior of adaptive filters in time-varying environments. The theoretical analysis establishes tighter bounds on the mean-squared error convergence rate, demonstrating that our derived conditions are less conservative than classical results by up to an order of magnitude. A key theoretical contribution is the development of a mean-square performance metric that accurately predicts filter behavior under various signal-to-noise ratios and eigenvalue spreads of the input correlation matrix. The framework successfully addresses long-standing open problems regarding the selection of step-size parameters and forgetting factors in non-stationary environments. Extensive numerical simulations confirm the theoretical predictions across diverse scenarios, validating the practical utility of the proposed analysis framework for the design and optimization of adaptive signal processing systems.

This paper proposes a novel attention-driven multimodal signal processing architecture that fundamentally transforms how image processing and speech processing systems integrate heterogeneous sensory information. Existing approaches treat different signal modalities as separate processing streams with late fusion, fundamentally limiting their ability to capture cross-modal dependencies and semantic correlations. The proposed architecture introduces a hierarchical attention mechanism that dynamically learns and aggregates complementary information from multiple signal sources at multiple abstraction levels. The system design incorporates learnable signal transformation modules that enable end-to-end optimization, eliminating the need for hand-crafted feature extraction and preprocessing pipelines that limit traditional approaches. We present a novel training methodology that addresses the challenge of learning from sparse and asynchronous multimodal data by introducing a curriculum learning strategy with modality-aware scheduling. The architecture demonstrates unprecedented performance in audiovisual speech recognition, multimodal emotion classification, and cross-modal retrieval tasks, outperforming existing methods by substantial margins. A critical innovation is the development of a modality-agnostic representation space that enables seamless knowledge transfer across different signal processing tasks. The proposed system represents a paradigm shift toward unified multimodal signal processing that mirrors the integrated nature of human perception.

This paper presents an advanced system design for biomedical signal processing that significantly improves the accuracy and robustness of neural activity classification from multichannel electrophysiological recordings. Existing systems struggle with the challenge of distinguishing between overlapping neural signals in high-density electrode arrays while maintaining real-time processing capabilities. The proposed system introduces a novel multirate signal processing pipeline that decomposes the raw biomedical signals into multiple temporal scales, enabling more effective extraction of neural features at different resolutions. We develop an optimized array processing configuration that adaptively reconfigures channel combinations based on signal characteristics, substantially improving spatial filtering performance compared to fixed array configurations. The system incorporates a lightweight neural network classifier specifically designed for deployment on resource-constrained biomedical hardware platforms, achieving classification accuracy comparable to cloud-based approaches while reducing computational requirements by approximately 70%. Critical improvements include enhanced robustness to electrode artifacts, motion-induced noise, and inter-subject variability through a novel domain adaptation module. Experimental validation on challenging clinical datasets demonstrates that the proposed system achieves state-of-the-art performance in seizure detection, motor intention classification, and neural prosthetic control, with significant improvements in both sensitivity and specificity metrics across diverse patient populations.
